newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Americas trade talks may leave controversy aside.
newsitem.headline: Americas trade talks may leave controversy aside.

text.p: Deputy trade ministers from 34 countries in the Americas meeting to discuss a regional free trade zone are likely to leave controversy aside and focus on areas of consensus, officials said Wednesday.

"It's important to remember that the talks don't end here but go on after Belo Horizonte," said a senior Brazilian Foreign Ministry official during a break in talks expected to continue long into the night in Rio de Janeiro.

Leaders of 34 countries in the Americas excluding Cuba decided at the Miami summit in 1994 to set up a Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA) by the year 2005, a trade zone that would stretch from Alaska to the plains of Patagonia.

Deputy trade ministers and other officials began meeting in Rio on Monday and will continue through till Thursday to prepare for a May 15-16 ministerial summit in the Brazilian city of Belo Horizonte.

On Wednesday it began to become clear that answers to the most controversial issues, such as the timetable and the structure for free trade talks, would not come out of either the Rio talks or the Belo Horizonte summit.

Jorge Campbell, secretary of international economic relations at the Argentine Foreign Ministry, said all had agreed to stick by the FTAA dream and to start formal negotiations after a presidential summit in Santiago, Chile, in March 1998.
They also agreed on the need to define now "what work remains to be done" by Santiago, he told reporters.

Brazilian Foreign Ministry sources said this basically meant producing a "minimum consensus" for a Ministerial Declaration to be signed at Belo Horizonte and leaving controversial issues to be settled by March 1998.
"Who in any case expected to solve everything here and now or even by Belo Horizonte," one of the sources said.

Canadian officials said virtually all parties except the Mercosur trade bloc grouping Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay and Paraguay had lined up behind a U.S. proposal to start discussing all aspects of trade liberalization at the same time.

"The most important thing is that we start the negotiations after Santiago. It doesn't mean that you start that day talking trade. People would have time to adjust," Peter Allgeier, chief U.S. negotiator at the Rio talks, told reporters.

Mercosur has stuck to its position that talks should begin on "business facilitation", basically the eradication of bureaucratic barriers to trade, then move on to subsidies and finally address the thorny issue of tariff reductions.
Yet despite differences, Allgeier said he was impressed at the enthusiasm for the FTAA being shown by participants.
Jose Botafogo Goncalves, general subsecretary of economic integration and trade at Brazil's Foreign Ministry, said delegates had decided to work late into the night Wednesday.
"Our intention is to advance as far as possible even though we know we have another day to talk," Botafogo told reporters.
